source_review.notes: Checked current primary Linux man-pages for signal concepts, sigaction, masks, synchronous waiting, atomic suspension, signal safety, signalfd, kill, pidfd signaling, and child waits, plus POSIX.1-2024 signal concepts. All 11 cited URLs returned HTTP 200; portable, Linux-specific, source-language, operational, and assurance claims are distinguished.

evidence: Checked signal s, disposition D(s), thread mask M_t, process-pending P_p, thread-pending P_t, real-time queue Q(s), authoritative state A, notification state N, progress k, remaining work r, and deadline T.
Reviewed generation, pending, delivery, disposition, mask, process- and thread-directed signaling, async-signal safety, standard coalescing, and real-time queue terminology.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation separates kernel notification state, target scope, application state, and interrupted-operation progress.

evidence: Executed five standard-signal generations against a coalescing pending-bit model and confirmed one pending bit and one handler run.
Confirmed the separately owned work queue drains all five authoritative items.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The deterministic illustration omits real signal delivery, threads, masks, memory order, handlers, queue limits, failures, and syscalls.

evidence: Re-derived deliverability from pending process or thread state plus an eligible thread whose mask does not block s.
Checked that retry advances by committed progress k and recomputes remaining time from absolute deadline T rather than replaying the original operation.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Disposition is modeled process-wide and blocking masks per thread, matching the cited signal contracts.

evidence: Reviewed generation before and after blocking, repeated standard signals, mixed targets, several eligible threads, pending disposition changes, uncatchable signals, unsafe handler reentry, errno changes, full self-pipe, spurious wait return, and check-then-sleep races.

Reviewed partial syscalls, EINTR, SA_RESTART limits, deadline extension, real-time queue exhaustion, timer coalescing, child bursts, fault recurrence, alternate-stack failure, fork and exec inheritance, PID reuse, repeated shutdown, overload, and wedged receivers.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Delivery, handler, waiting, interruption, timer, child, fault, identity, lifecycle, security, operational, and assurance boundaries receive distinct treatment.

evidence: Traced single-owner masks, atomic waits, async-safe handler state, coalescing-independent work, partial progress, identity-safe targeting, and lifecycle policy through ten examples and five answers.
Verified the toy intentionally collapses five generations into one notification while retaining and draining five authoritative items.
invariant_checking.notes: The chapter does not conflate generation with delivery, notification with acknowledgment, disposition with mask, thread safety with async safety, standard pending state with a counter, or restart with idempotency.

evidence: Reviewed inventory, ownership, coalescing, handler handoff, atomic waiting, partial progress, lifecycle, overload, authority, and timing-evidence obligations.

Constructed counterexamples for handler logging, inconsistent worker masks, check-then-pause, discarded read prefix, one-shot child wait, full self-pipe, real-time queue exhaustion, reused PID, returning to an unresolved fault, and complex repeated termination.
proof_review.notes: The chapter supplies reusable signal-control obligations, not a formal proof of a handler, runtime, supervisor, event loop, process-identity system, or real-time response bound.

evidence: Audited uses of atomic, safe, pending, delivered, queued, ordered, restarted, reliable, fatal, bounded, and certification.

Confirmed POSIX and Linux guarantees, source-language handler constraints, abstract notification state, toy coalescing, operational timing, security authority, and human assurance remain separately scoped.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Synchronous acceptance and signalfd are not presented as unlimited queues, and the toy is not presented as operating-system behavior evidence.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/OS-028/report.json records generated count, pending bits, handler runs, and drained work for toy-signal-coalescing under Python 3.
Reviewed delivery delay, coalescing-sensitive state, wake overflow, interruptions, retries, child status, shutdown stage, deadlines, kernel, runtime, topology, raw results, and probe effects.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The passing toy excludes signals, syscalls, scheduler timing, threads, resource limits, and application failure.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed generation, pending state, delivery, dispositions, masks, standard and real-time signals, async handlers, self-pipes, synchronous acceptance, atomic waits, signalfd, interruptions, timers, children, faults, targeting, job control, fork and exec, shutdown, observability, security, and assurance as coupled concepts.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed sigaction, pthread-style masking, sigwaitinfo, sigsuspend, pselect-style waits, self-pipes, signalfd, partial syscall progress, absolute deadlines, SIGCHLD drains, alternate stacks, kill and pidfd identity, close-on-exec, and supervisor behavior as implementable concerns. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from signal state and ownership through handler constraints, synchronous integration, interruption, timers, process lifecycle, shutdown, security, and evidence, followed by nine trade-offs, fourteen misconceptions, ten examples, and five complete exercises.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external operating-systems academic, POSIX or Linux signal maintainer, runtime or supervisor implementer, event-loop or real-time specialist, security or safety authority, independent verifier, or certification review is claimed.
